c.tagline: Thailand's laid-back northern capital of golden temples, misty mountains, and digital nomads.

taxi.fareNote: Red songthaew shared trucks are the everyday local taxi — flag one down, state your destination, and expect about 30-60 baht per person for short hops agreed before you ride; tuk-tuks and Grab/Bolt are the easy alternatives, as metered street taxis are scarce.

emergency.note: Tourist Police 1155 has English-speaking operators; 191 reaches police and 1669 the ambulance/medical service.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_landmark.Riverside (Wat Ket): Ping River Wat Ket, Chiang Mai
hood_landmark.Night Bazaar (Chang Khlan): Chiang Mai Night Bazaar, Chang Khlan

avoid.reason: Scooter rental-damage scams and road-accident risk; heavy smoke/haze Mar–Apr

hood_desc: The moat-ringed historic heart, packed with centuries-old temples like Wat Phra Singh and Wat Chedi Luang and lined with quiet lanes, guesthouses, and cafes; the classic base for first-time visitors who want everything walkable.

Chiang Mai's trendy west-side district of hip cafes, art galleries, wine bars, co-working spaces, and boutiques near Chiang Mai University; the hub for digital nomads and a younger, design-conscious crowd.
The leafy east bank of the Ping River around Wat Ket, lined with old teak houses, riverside restaurants, and five-star resorts; a relaxed, scenic area for slower stays.
An up-and-coming local neighborhood just north of the Old City between it and Nimman, full of fresh markets, cheap eats, and affordable rooms; a favorite of budget travelers and long-stay expats.
The commercial strip east of the Old City built around the sprawling nightly Night Bazaar on Chang Khlan Road, with big hotels, massage parlors, bars, and shopping; lively and central but touristy.

water.note: Drink bottled or filtered water rather than tap.

transit.pay: Pay songthaews and tuk-tuks in cash directly to the driver — around 30-60 baht per person for short hops, agreed before you ride; RTC city buses cost about 30 baht flat (cash or QR). There is no rechargeable transit card system.
transit.hours: Red songthaews and tuk-tuks run informally through the day and into the night; the RTC city bus network runs roughly 6:00 AM to 11:00 PM, with Grab and Bolt filling the late-night gap.
transit.note: Chiang Mai has no metro, tram, or urban rail; getting around means red songthaew shared trucks (the local workhorse), a small RTC city bus network, tuk-tuks, and ride-hailing apps.

bus: Arcade (Chang Phueak) bus terminal for intercity coaches to Bangkok, Chiang Rai, and Pai

car.idp: Required (International Driving Permit needed alongside your home license)

train: Chiang Mai Railway Station (State Railway of Thailand line to Bangkok via Phitsanulok and Ayutthaya)

transit.m: RTC airport shuttle bus to the Old City / Night Bazaar (~20-30 min)
Airport flat-rate taxi to the city center (150-200 baht, 15-25 min)

tip.r: Not expected; rounding up the bill or leaving 20-40 baht for good service at restaurants is appreciated but not required.

food.name: Khao soi
food.desc: The dish Chiang Mai is built on: egg noodles in coconut curry broth, crowned with a fried noodle nest, pickled mustard greens and lime.

places.name: Khao Soi Khun Yai
places.area: Sri Poom, near Wat Phra Singh
places.note: Grandma's khao soi, down an alley behind the temple; thick, creamy and sold out by early afternoon.

places.name: Khao Soi Mae Sai
places.note: Local institution with thousands of reviews; open mornings to late afternoon only.

places.name: Khao Soi Lung Prakit Kad Kom
places.note: Famous for a beef khao soi heaped with tender braised meat; featured on Somebody Feed Phil.

food.name: Khao kha moo
food.desc: Pork leg stewed for hours in five-spice and soy until it falls apart, ladled over rice with pickled greens and a boiled egg.

places.name: Khao Kha Moo Chang Phueak (Cowboy Hat Lady)
places.note: The city's most famous stall, now with a daytime shopfront as well as the night stall.

places.name: Chang Phueak Night Market
places.note: The whole strip outside the old-city gate does pork leg rice after dark.

food.name: Sai ua
food.desc: Northern Thai herb sausage packed with lemongrass, galangal, kaffir lime leaf and red curry paste, grilled over charcoal and sliced.

places.name: Warorot Market
places.note: Dozens of sausage vendors let you taste before you buy; the city's sai ua headquarters.

places.name: Chiang Mai Gate Market
places.note: Evening grills selling sai ua by the coil alongside sticky rice and nam prik.

food.name: Nam prik ong and nam prik num
food.desc: Two northern chilli dips, one tomato-and-pork red, one smoky roasted green chilli, scooped up with crackling and steamed vegetables.

places.name: Huen Phen
places.note: Forty-plus years of old family recipes; the classic sit-down northern Thai meal.

places.name: Tong Tem Toh
places.note: Busy garden restaurant that made northern chilli dips accessible to visitors.

food.name: Gaeng hang lay
food.desc: Burmese-influenced pork belly curry, sweet-sour with tamarind, ginger and peanuts and almost no chilli heat. Eaten with sticky rice.

places.name: Huen Muan Jai
places.note: Local-favourite northern kitchen, consistently named for the best hang lay in town.

places.name: Huen Phen
places.note: Serves the full northern spread, hang lay included, in a cluttered antique dining room.

food.name: Khanom jeen nam ngiao
food.desc: Rice noodles in a tomato and pork-rib broth flavoured with fermented soybean and dried kapok flower. Northern Thailand's other great noodle soup.

places.name: Chiang Mai Gate Market
places.note: Morning and evening noodle stalls ladling nam ngiao for well under 50 baht.

places.name: Huen Muan Jai
places.note: Sit-down version of the market classic, with the full tray of herbs and pickles.

food.name: Cha yen
food.desc: Thai iced milk tea, brewed strong and spiced then poured over crushed ice with condensed milk. Best from a market cart, not a chain.

places.name: Charlie Thai Tea
places.note: Small modern tea bar where you pick the leaf and dial the sweetness down.

places.name: Warorot Market
places.note: Old tea carts pulling cha yen all day amid the sausage and snack stalls.

food.name: Northern Thai single-origin coffee
food.desc: Arabica grown in the hills around Chiang Mai and Chiang Rai, roasted in town. Chiang Mai has one of Asia's best small coffee scenes.

places.name: Ristr8to
places.note: World latte-art champion baristas; the cafe that put Chiang Mai coffee on the map.

places.name: Akha Ama Coffee
places.note: Grower-owned roaster buying direct from Akha hill farms north of the city.

landmarks: Wat Phra That Doi Suthep
Perched on a mountain above the city, this glittering gold-chedi temple reached by a 306-step naga staircase is northern Thailand's holiest and most iconic sight.
Wat Chedi Luang
A colossal 15th-century brick chedi, partially toppled by earthquake, dominates the old city and once housed Thailand's revered Emerald Buddha.
Wat Phra Singh
Chiang Mai's most venerated temple shelters the Phra Singh Buddha within exquisite Lanna-style gilded halls and the jewel-box Lai Kham viharn's murals.
Tha Phae Gate and the Old City walls
The restored eastern gateway of the 700-year-old moated city walls is Chiang Mai's symbolic heart, gateway to temples, cafes, and Sunday market crowds.
Sunday Walking Street Market (Ratchadamnoen Road)
Every Sunday evening the old city's main artery becomes a kilometer-long feast of Lanna handicrafts, street food, and musicians beneath lantern-lit temple walls.
Doi Inthanon National Park
Thailand's highest peak crowns this misty day-trip park of waterfalls, hill-tribe villages, cloud forest trails, and the twin royal pagodas with panoramic gardens.
Wat Umong Suan Phutthatham
A 700-year-old forest monastery honeycombed with meditation tunnels beneath a mossy chedi, offering a serene, wooded contrast to the city's gilded temples.
Wat Suan Dok
Whitewashed royal mausoleums cluster beside a 48-meter golden chedi at this 14th-century temple, famously photogenic at sunset and home to monk chats.
Wat Sri Suphan (Silver Temple)
In the silversmiths' district of Wualai, this dazzling ordination hall is sheathed entirely in hammered silver and aluminum, glinting spectacularly under evening lights.
Warorot Market (Kad Luang)
Chiang Mai's great local bazaar by the Ping River overflows with northern sausages, textiles, flowers, and hill-tribe goods, a sensory plunge into Lanna daily life.

train.note: Chiang Mai is the northern terminus of the State Railway of Thailand and no train from here crosses a border - Thailand's international rail links are far away at Padang Besar for Malaysia and Nong Khai for Laos. The station is about 3 km east of the old city, and services run to Bangkok's Krung Thep Aphiwat in 12 to 15 hours, with two daytime trains and around four overnight sleepers. Second-class air-conditioned sleepers sell out first, so book ahead; tickets go on sale up to 180 days out. From outside Thailand use the official SRT D-Ticket site, which needs an account, rejects special characters in the registration form, requires booking at least three days ahead and sells only first and second-class air-con sleepers.

bus.note: Long-distance coaches use Arcade Bus Station (Terminals 2 and 3) on Kaeo Nawarat Road northeast of the old city, with Green Bus (https://web.greenbusthailand.com/en) covering the whole north and even a 24-hour run to Phuket, and Nakhonchai Air and the state BKS operator running to Bangkok in about 9 to 12 hours. No scheduled international coach leaves Chiang Mai under a single bookable operator: for Laos take a Green Bus or minibus to Chiang Khong (about 6 hours), cross the Fourth Thai-Lao Friendship Bridge on the shuttle, and pick up a Lao bus at Huay Xai, where PLS Company runs services on into Laos and China. Through Chiang Mai to Luang Prabang tickets of roughly 18 hours are sold by agents in town, but they are agency products rather than one carrier's route. Most nationalities get a Lao visa on arrival at the bridge; bring US dollars in cash and a passport photo.

ferry.note: Chiang Mai is inland in the northern mountains, so there are no sea ferries and the only boats in town are sightseeing and dinner cruises on the Ping River. The classic water route out of the region is the Mekong slow boat, which leaves from Huay Xai in Laos - about 6 hours away by bus to Chiang Khong plus the border crossing - and takes two days downriver to Luang Prabang with an overnight stop at Pakbeng. Departures moved to around 09:00, so you normally have to overnight in Chiang Khong or Huay Xai first rather than connecting the same day. More comfortable two-day cruises on the same stretch are run by Shompoo Cruise (https://shompoo-cruise.com/en/) and Nagi of Mekong.

half.name: Chiang Dao
half.blurb: A limestone mountain and cave system north of the city, with a sacred Buddhist cave temple and hiking trails.

half.name: Lampang
half.blurb: A former teak-trade town famous for its horse-drawn carriages and the striking Burmese-Lanna temple Wat Phra That Lampang Luang.

half.name: Mae Kampong Village
half.blurb: A misty hillside community built on stilts along a mountain stream, known for organic tea and homestay tourism.

half.name: Bo Sang
half.blurb: A village dedicated to handmade paper umbrellas and fans, where artisans still paint and assemble them by hand.

full.name: Pai
full.blurb: A laid-back mountain town reached via a famously winding road, with hot springs, canyons and a bohemian night market.
